title: Overview
text:
This page will show the map of topics for this course: which concepts there are, how they build on each other, and where each one appears in the experiments. Until the map is ready, here are the concepts that already have a page of their own:

A Brief History of AI: seventy-five years of artificial intelligence, compiled live by an AI agent.
AI Agents: a language model that uses tools in a loop to reach a goal.

title: A Brief History of AI
text:
When did artificial intelligence begin: in 1950 with Alan Turing, in 1956 at a workshop in Dartmouth, or in 2022 with ChatGPT? Instead of answering from a slide, we collect what you already know on a pinboard and hand it to an AI agent. The agent researches every milestone, reads the sources, checks last year’s list for errors, and turns the result into an interactive timeline with a quiz.
What the agent does along the way is the programme of this course:

How can a model read a photo of handwriting?
How does a language model write a plan, code and text?
Why does it use tools, and when are rules better than learning?
Can we trust facts an AI has checked?
What happens when an agent splits its work among sub-agents, or publishes on its own?

title: AI Agents
text:
A chatbot answers, and you take the next step yourself: you copy the code, run it, paste back the error. An agent takes those steps on its own. Under the hood it is the same language model; the difference is what is built around it. A working definition: an LLM agent runs tools in a loop to achieve a goal.
Everything else, the plan, the instructions it loads, the sub-agents, the context it keeps in mind, is built around that loop. This page answers:

What is the difference between a chatbot and an agent?
What are the parts of an agent, and what does each one do?
When is an agent the right choice, and when is a fixed workflow better?
Why are agents suddenly everywhere?
What can go wrong when an agent acts with your permissions?

title: AI Agents
text:
Explanation

The model, the tools, the loop
The language model can only produce text. It cannot open a file or load a web page. What it can do is write down which tool it wants to call, and with which arguments: read a file, write a file, run a command, search the web. A program on your computer executes the call and hands the result back to the model. Then the model decides what to do next. This loop, think, act, observe, repeats until the goal is reached. In research the pattern is known as ReAct (Yao et al., 2022).


Context, plans and sub-agents
Everything the agent “knows” during a task sits in its context window: the goal, every tool result, every intermediate thought. When it fills up, the agent has to summarise or forget. To stay on track, agents write themselves a plan, a to-do list they tick off, and read instructions stored in text files when they need them. For big tasks they can start sub-agents: copies of themselves, each with a fresh context window, working in parallel.


Workflow or agent?
Not everything with AI inside is an agent. A workflow follows predefined steps; an agent decides the next step itself. The advice from Anthropic: keep it as simple as possible, and use agents only where the task needs that freedom.


Handle with care
An agent acts with your permissions. It can read every file you can read, run every command you can run, and publish to the internet. Whoever gives an agent access hands over their own keys. Asking it to show its plan before it acts is where you stay in control.

title: Be the Agent
text: An AI agent such as Claude Code gets a goal instead of a recipe. It plans its own steps, uses tools and keeps going until the job is done. In this experiment you play such an agent yourselves, with cards, a calculator and a few printed pages instead of a computer. One of you is the language model, one is everything around it, and one watches and keeps the log. By the end you will have run, by hand, the loop that every AI agent runs on.

title: Be the Agent
text:
Goal
Find out from the inside how an agent works: what the language model decides, what the tools do, and why everything the model knows has to be on its stack of cards.

title: Be the Agent
text:
What you need

A group of three. In a group of four, two of you share the Toolbox.
The kit at the end of this document, printed and cut out: the system card, three task cards, the farm files, the web pages, the rules for the Toolbox and the Observer’s sheet.
A stack of blank index cards, a pen for everyone and a calculator.
About 30 minutes for the first two tasks.

title: Be the Agent
text:
The three roles








Role
What you do
What you may look at




Model
You decide what happens next and write it on a card.
Only the stack of cards in front of you.


Toolbox
You carry out exactly what a tool card says and write the result on a new card.
The farm files, the web pages and the calculator.


Observer
You keep the log: every card in order, with a note on what happened.
Everything, but you never help.

title: Be the Agent
text:
The rules

The Model sees only its stack. It never looks at the farm files or the web pages, and nobody talks to it. Everything it learns arrives on a card.
Every card the Model writes starts with one of three words:

THINK: a note to itself, for example THINK: I need the size of the field first.
TOOL: a tool call, written exactly as on the system card, for example TOOL: read_file("fields").
ANSWER: the answer to the task. This card ends the game.

The Toolbox carries out a tool card literally and writes the result on a new card that starts with RESULT:. If the tool does not exist or the call is written wrongly, the result is an error. The Toolbox never repairs a call, never guesses what the Model meant and never adds anything that was not asked for.
Every card goes on top of the stack in the order it was written, and it stays there.
One card per turn. The Model writes one card; if it is a tool card, the Toolbox answers it before the Model writes the next one.

title: Be the Agent
text:
Steps

Set up. The Model’s stack starts with the system card, with the card for Task 1 on top of it. The Toolbox lays out the farm files and the web pages where the Model cannot see them. The Observer takes the log sheet.
Play Task 1. How many cards did it take? Did the Model write a THINK: card before its first tool call?
Swap roles and play Task 2. Which tools did the Model use, and in which order? Did the first search find the right page? Which value did the Model choose, and how did it decide?
Count. The Observer reads the log aloud: rounds, tool calls, errors, and how many cards lie on the stack at the end.
Play Task 3 if there is time. One thing in the farm files will only be noticed by a careful Model.
Compare with a real agent. Your lecturer shows the log of a real agent session. Find the places where it thinks, calls a tool, receives a result and answers.

title: Be the Agent
text:
What you just played







In the game
In a real AI agent




the stack of cards
the context window: everything the model knows during a task


the system card
the system prompt: who the model is and which tools it has


the task card
the user’s prompt, the goal


a THINK: card
the model’s reasoning or plan


a TOOL: card
a tool call: the model only writes text, a program carries it out


the Toolbox
the harness, the program around the model that runs the tools


a RESULT: card
the observation: the tool’s result, added to the context


the Observer’s log
the transcript of the session


the ANSWER: card
the stop condition: the goal is reached



The loop you ran, think, act and observe until the goal is reached, is the loop inside every AI agent. The Model never opened a file and never pressed a key on the calculator; it only wrote text, and something else carried it out.

title: Be the Agent
text:
Go further

Limited memory. The stack may now hold at most eight cards. When it is full, the Model writes a SUMMARY: card that replaces the oldest cards; the system card and the task card always stay. Play Task 3 again. What got lost, and did it matter?
Be the tool for a chatbot. Solve Task 2 with a chatbot in your browser. Whenever it needs a file, a web page or a calculation, you have to provide it yourself. Who is the Toolbox now, and who decides the next step?
A new tool. Invent a sixth tool, for example forecast("date"), add its description to the system card and write a page for the Toolbox. Does the Model use the new tool without being told to?
A wrong result. The Toolbox secretly returns one wrong result, for example a calculation that is off by a factor of ten. Does the Model notice? What would a real agent need in order to notice?

title: Be the Agent
text:
Reflection
Write down your own answers first, then discuss them in your group.

In which round would the Model have been stuck without the Toolbox’s cards?
What would have gone differently if the Model had had to give up its stack after ten cards?
Who did the thinking, who did the acting, and which of it could the Model actually do?

title: Be the Agent
text:
System card






NoteSYSTEM



You are the assistant of Greenfield Farm. You can only act by writing cards. On every turn, write exactly one card that starts with THINK:, TOOL: or ANSWER:.
You can use these tools:

search("words") finds pages on the web and returns their titles
open("title") returns the full text of one web page
read_file("name") returns one of the farm’s files: fields, soil_tests, stock, weather
calculator("expression") calculates, for example calculator("4.5 * 100")
write_file("name", "text") saves a text as a new file of the farm

When you have answered the task, write ANSWER: and stop.

This page is no longer updated. Recommended nitrogen for winter wheat: 210 kg N/ha; for winter barley: 190 kg N/ha.








TipSplitting nitrogen in winter wheat



Keywords: wheat, nitrogen, split, dose, timing, first
Winter wheat gets its nitrogen in three doses: the first dose, 40 % of the total, at the start of growth in spring; the second, 40 %, when the stem starts to grow; the third, 20 %, when the ears appear.








TipWhen may fertiliser be spread? — teaching rules



Keywords: when, date, rules, ban, spreading, frozen, snow, fertiliser
No nitrogen fertiliser may be spread between 1 October and 31 January. At any time of year, fertiliser must never be spread on ground that is frozen, flooded or covered in snow.

Calcium ammonium nitrate contains 27 % nitrogen: 100 kg of product bring 27 kg of nitrogen to the field.








TipWinter wheat varieties 2026



Keywords: wheat, varieties, yield, 2026
Twelve new varieties were tested this year. The highest yields came from varieties with good winter hardiness and resistance to yellow rust.

title: Artificial Intelligence
text:
Everybody talks about AI agents: programs that get a goal instead of a recipe, plan their own steps, use tools, and keep going until the job is done. You will watch one at work, try one yourself, and then open it up, layer by layer.
We start at the top, with the agent you have just seen in action, and work our way down: to the language model inside it, to how that model represents text and meaning, to how it was trained, and finally to the simple idea of learning from data. Then we climb back up and ask what all this means for your field and for the rest of us.
Every session starts with an experiment. You do something first and understand it afterwards, often with pen, paper and a table before any computer comes in. All experiments can be repeated at home. Where there is code to write, you don’t type it yourself: you tell an AI agent what you need and check what it builds.
